1.pericope_label: Abimelech buys a following and murders his brethren

schools.summary: Gill explains that Abimelech had been reared at Ophrah though his mother lived at Shechem, so that this was a visit to his uncles, and cannot settle the value of the silver, shekels seeming too small a sum to raise a party and talents far too large for such a city; he suspects the number was chosen to answer the number of Gideon's sons.

Henry traces the ambition to the mother's instilling and to a name that carried royalty in it, and insists that Abimelech had no call from God as Gideon had and that the proposal came from nobody but himself. He holds that none of Gideon's sons ever intended to reign, and that those who design ill are readiest to suspect others of it; he calls the hired men the scum of the country and says like leader like followers; he judges a man who made himself a pensioner to an idol unfit ever to defend Israel; he sees in the massacre what ambition makes of a man and what peril attaches to high birth, concluding that the lower the safer; and he notes that God was never consulted about a king, that the Shechemites rewarded the murder with a diadem, and that the rest of Israel never stirred.

Clarke explains the visit as an attempt to be proclaimed governor in his father's room, grants the rhetorical force of asking whether seventy tyrants are better than one, observes that a man with no right to govern must support his usurpation by whatever means come to hand, and describes the hired men as worthless and dissolute persons living on the public with nothing to lose, by the cunning management of whom most revolutions have been brought about.

Ellicott reads the chapter as an illustration of slow but certain retribution, Gideon's polygamy and unauthorised worship being punished through the Canaanite kin of his base-born son, in whom he traces the father's courage overshadowed by the mother's stock; he renders the men of Shechem as lords, a Canaanite rather than Hebrew title, describes a mixed population in armed neutrality with the Israelites placed much as the Normans among the English, calls the charge against Gideon's sons a calumny, compares the plea of bone and flesh to that of a Norman king born of a Saxon mother, marks the massacre as the first scriptural instance of a custom later followed by Baasha, Zimri, Jehu and Athaliah, and notes that the coronation took place at the terebinth of Joshua's stone of witness. Keil and Delitzsch identify the silver as temple treasure applied, as often, to political ends, and hear in the one stone an omen of the northern kingdom later founded at Shechem, where each dynasty exterminated the last.

debates: Whether Gideon's sons had any designs on the government. Henry and Ellicott both deny it flatly, Ellicott adding that Gideon had expressly repudiated such rule; Clarke allows the rhetorical force of Abimelech's question without endorsing its premise.

What the seventy pieces of silver were. Gill rejects both shekels as too little and talents as too much and inclines to pounds; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott are content with shekels drawn from the temple treasury.

How the massacre should be classified. Ellicott makes it the first scriptural example of a standing Oriental practice and traces its later imitators; Keil and Delitzsch read it as an omen of the dynastic murders of the northern kingdom; Henry as a lesson on the perils of high birth.
outliers: Ellicott's note that an ancient temple served at once as sanctuary, fortress and bank, the hoard at Delphi having financed a sacred war.
Ellicott's observation that the coronation took place beside the very stone Joshua had set up as a witness of faithfulness.
Henry's remark that none would have dreamed of making such a man king if he had not dreamed of it himself.
themes: a name that carried a crown in it
seventy tyrants or one
an army bought from an idol's treasury
seventy men on one stone

7.pericope_label: Jotham on Gerizim: the fable of the trees

schools.summary: Gill calls the fable the most ancient of its kind, framed seven hundred years before Aesop and exceeding anything of his, takes the trees for Israel generally and the Shechemites in particular, and notes that no tree is named before the bramble but a fruitful one, and only such as were best known in that country.

Henry marks this as the only testimony borne against the confederacy and takes the absence of prophet or judgment for a sign that God had departed from the people, observing that Jotham neither raised an army nor claimed anything for himself, which refutes the slander against Gideon's sons. He reads the refusals as a compliment to Gideon and the earlier judges and as showing that wise men prefer being useful to being great, since there was no occasion for a king at all, the application was made to fruit-bearers rather than to the stately cedar, and office costs a man his private advantages and endangers his fruitfulness. He calls the bramble worthless and hurtful, beginning with the curse and ending in fire, notes that this election alone was unanimous, and mocks the invitation to trust in its shadow; and he has Jotham plead a father who fought at the hazard of his life, contrast the murdered sons who honoured his name with the one who blemished it, and leave the issue to providence.

Clarke calls it the oldest and without exception the best fable in the world, supports the possibility of Jotham's being heard from a traveller in southern India who heard men converse from hill to hill without shouting, would render the disputed word gods rather than God on the ground that the parable was accommodated to Shechemite idolatry, and treats the bramble's promise as the vain boast of a would-be sovereign, all promise and no performance, its threat being a strong figure since the smallest fire reduces a bramble to ashes.

Ellicott doubts that Jotham stood on the actual summit and prefers a precipitous crag above the town, testifies from his own experience how far the Oriental chanting delivery carries in that air, explains how Jotham dared the risk, and notes that Josephus places it at a public feast; he observes that this chapter yields the first Israelite king, the first massacre of brethren and the first fable at once, that Scripture holds only one other; he allows that the disputed clause may mean that gods and men honour these things in the olive, identifies the bramble as the buckthorn addressed in a blunt imperative, marks the ironic echo of the bramble's own phrase in the application, and calls the son of his maidservant intentionally contemptuous though the woman was no slave. Keil and Delitzsch describe Gerizim rising as a steep wall of rock some eight hundred feet above the valley and treat the parable as genuinely prophetic.

debates: Whether Jotham could have been heard. Keil and Delitzsch give the height of the rock without comment; Ellicott denies the actual summit was possible and appeals to the carrying power of the Oriental chant; Clarke supports the possibility from a modern traveller's report of hill-to-hill conversation.

What the clause about honouring God and man means. Clarke would translate it gods, holding the parable accommodated to Shechemite idolatry; Ellicott allows either that reading or the sense that gods and men honour these things in the olive, and refers it in either case to the use of oil in sacrifice.

How the fable ranks. Gill dates it seven hundred years before Aesop and rates it above him; Clarke calls it the best in the world; Ellicott sets it among the firsts of this chapter and notes that Scripture contains only one other.
outliers: Ellicott's explanation of how Jotham survived the speech — a crag above a hillside of caves, possible partisans, and the pathos of his opening.
Henry's observation that the bramble's election was the only unanimous one in the fable.
themes: a voice from the mountain
trees that would rather bear fruit
trust in the shadow of a thorn
an appeal left to providence

22.pericope_label: The evil spirit between Abimelech and Shechem, and the rise of Gaal

schools.summary: Gill thinks it amazing that Israel acquiesced in the usurpation instead of rising as one man to avenge the sons of Gideon, and observes that the reign proved short, as the reigns of wicked princes often are.

Henry notes that Abimelech is never said to have judged Israel or done his country any service, holding the title only, and that the triumphing of the wicked is short; he reads the discord as God permitting the great mischief-maker to sow it while their own lusts served as evil spirits in their hearts, and lays down that when a man's sin is made his punishment God is not the author of the sin though the punishment is from him. From the charge of blood he draws that God makes inquisition for innocent blood, that accessories are reckoned with as well as principals, and that confederates in wickedness are justly dashed one against another, blood being no lasting cement. He sees the Shechemites making him their prisoner whom they had made their prince, notes that Abimelech and Gaal were each the son of a servant so that one bramble contested with another, presses the irony that the temple which financed the king became the room where he was cursed, and judges that Gaal sought not liberty but only a change of tyrant.

Clarke keeps the evil spirit at the level of providence, God permitting jealousies which bred factions and factions insurrections and slaughter, observes that God punished Abimelech by the very persons who had raised him and often makes the instruments of men's sins the means of their punishment, places the ambush on the road between Shechem and Ophrah where the robbers plundered all comers, and calls his wish that the people were under his hand the language of a sly and hypocritical demagogue.

Ellicott is cautious whether the evil spirit denotes a being or a disposition, stresses the divine Nemesis on bloodshed, explains that the ambush need not have been meant to seize him and that disaffection in Palestine has always shown itself in brigandage, takes Gaal for a Canaanite freebooter whose name as we have it may be a contemptuous distortion, calls the feast a heathen analogue of the Ingathering, would render the verb abused rather than cursed, and unpacks Gaal's taunts — the sneer after the manner of Nabal, the obscure clause that follows, and the point that a son of Jerubbaal is connected with neither Ephraimites nor Canaanites. Keil and Delitzsch insist the verb means to govern rather than to reign, since this was a despotism and not a monarchy, limit Israel to the tribes that acknowledged him, argue for a real demon under Satan's influence rather than a mere temper and explain the use of Elohim by the reference to divine justice, take Gaal for the captain of a band of freebooters, and identify the offerings as the praise-offerings of a fourth-year vintage.

debates: What the evil spirit was. Keil and Delitzsch argue for a real demon sent under divine commission; Ellicott leaves open whether the word means a being or a disposition; Clarke reduces it to permitted jealousies; Henry combines the two, making men's own lusts the evil spirits while the punishment remains from God.

Who Gaal was. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take him for a freebooting captain, Ellicott adding that he was probably Canaanite and that his name may be a distortion; Clarke makes him a Canaanite bent on restoring the house of Hamor; Henry is content to note that he and Abimelech were both sons of servants.

What the phrase about the liers in wait implies. Clarke and Henry read it as a plot on Abimelech's person; Ellicott denies that it need mean so much and treats the episode as ordinary brigandage born of disaffection.
outliers: Clarke's observation that God punished Abimelech by the very men who had raised him.
Henry's point that the temple whose treasury bought Abimelech his crown became the room in which he was cursed — how should Satan cast out Satan?
Keil and Delitzsch's identification of the feast as the praise-offerings due from a vineyard's fourth-year fruit.
themes: a rule that was never a reign
an evil spirit sent between allies
blood as no lasting cement
one bramble against another

30.pericope_label: Zebul betrays Gaal, and Abimelech routs him

schools.summary: Gill notes that Abimelech had set Zebul over the city, gives both the crafty sense of the disputed adverb and the reading which makes it a place-name, and records that Abimelech withdrew to Arumah rather than forcing an entry.

Henry observes that Zebul's anger was the hotter because Gaal had spoken slightingly of him, and guesses a little flattery might have bought him; he remarks that betrayers are often betrayed by their own, that the cursing of a king is strangely carried by a bird of the air, and asks how Shechem could hope to prosper with its own ruler in the enemy's interest. In the answer about the shadow he finds both a ridicule of a man ready to fight with a shadow and a device to hold him in talk; in the later upbraiding he sees proud people made to change their note and dread those they had most despised, Gaal being challenged in the very terms he had used; and he has Gaal disheartened and beaten, with the loss falling on the townsmen, as it commonly does in popular tumults where the multitude are drawn into snares by men who promise glorious success.

Clarke reads the report that they fortify the city as meaning that under pretence of repairing the walls they were putting it in a state of defence, or else seducing the inhabitants from their loyalty, supposes Gaal had got some intimation of what was afoot, and reports the alternative renderings of the second landmark — the way of the oaks, or of the magicians and regarders of the times — supposing it a place where augurs and soothsayers lived.

Ellicott takes Zebul's title to suggest a military commandant, says the disputed adverb occurs nowhere else and the versions differ but that the message was plainly secret, would render the report as tyrannising over the city rather than fortifying it, explains the ambush as meant to catch the Shechemites finishing their vintage, notes that the gate was the ordinary station of rulers though Gaal went there to keep a look-out, observes that the shadow would advance as the sun rose and that Zebul speaks as if Gaal were still intoxicated from his feast, confesses Zebul's position anomalous and the narrative too brief to explain it, takes the navel of the land for a swelling hill and renders the second place the Enchanters' Terebinth, offers expostulation as an alternative to taunt in the upbraiding, insists that Gaal led the citizens rather than merely fighting in their sight, calls the victory complete, declines to identify Arumah with Arimathea, and passes on Josephus's account that Zebul expelled Gaal by accusing him of cowardice. Keil and Delitzsch report that the adverb may mean with deceit or may be a misspelt place-name, note the four companies laid in ambush, render the phrase as coming from the navel of the land and the wizard's terebinths, have Zebul declare openly against Gaal, and deny that Gaal led the citizens since only his own retinue was with him.

debates: What the adverb describing Zebul's message means. Keil and Delitzsch report both a sense of deceit and a place-name; Gill gives both; Ellicott says the versions differ and settles only for secrecy.

Whether Gaal led the Shechemites out. Keil and Delitzsch deny it, since only his own retinue was with him, and take the phrase to mean he fought while the lords looked on; Ellicott insists he led them.

How Zebul's question about Gaal's mouth should be read. Keil and Delitzsch and Henry take it as an open reproach once the mask was off; Ellicott offers instead an expostulation against past rashness, unless Zebul was already safe from Gaal's vengeance.
outliers: Henry's remark that betrayers are often betrayed by some among themselves, and that the cursing of a king is strangely carried by a bird of the air.
Clarke's suggestion that the place named at Gaal's second sighting was one where augurs and soothsayers lived.
Josephus's account, cited by Ellicott, that Zebul got rid of Gaal by charging him with cowardice and mismanagement.
themes: a governor who kept his own counsel
the shadow of the mountains
where is now thy mouth
a city that lost its champion

42.pericope_label: Shechem destroyed, and the tower burnt over its refugees

schools.summary: Gill identifies the men with Abimelech as his forces from Arumah and notes that the word for his company may mean the heads, great men being among them; he infers from their being said only to have heard the news that the tower stood outside the city though near it, identifies it with the house of Millo so that this part of Jotham's curse was now accomplished, describes Zalmon as a mountain near Shechem named from the shade of its trees, and pictures the column returning with boughs on their shoulders like men that were trees walking.

Clarke denies that the salt was meant to make the ground sterile, since nobody would think of cultivating a city, and holds that salt being an emblem of incorruption and perpetuity it was strewn to perpetuate the memorial of the deed and to signify that the desolation was meant to be everlasting, citing the custom in other nations and the razing of Milan in the twelfth century; he takes the hold to mean the precincts of the temple, since a thousand men and women were gathered there together.

Ellicott can give no reason why there were three companies this time rather than four, infers a ruthlessly vindictive temper from the slaughter of husbandmen who were no armed host, notes that Abimelech intercepted the people before they could regain the city and kept the post of honour and danger for himself, reads the salt as devoting the city to barrenness and as showing his execration against the populace who had raised him, cites Milan and the salting of Coligny's house, calls the refugees the garrison of the house of Millo and canvasses the versions on the word for hold, explains Zalmon as the nearest source of wood and as meaning shady, observes that the text speaks of axes rather than one axe, recalls the bough-bearing scene in Macbeth, and marks the fulfilment of Jotham's words, comparing Zimri burnt in the palace at Tirzah. Keil and Delitzsch take the morning movement for ordinary field-work rather than war, have Abimelech's own division block the gate while the other two fell on the people in the open, read the salt as declaring the place a barren desert for ever, explain that the men of the tower sought sanctuary with their god rather than a defensible position, and narrate the piling of branches and the death of about a thousand.

debates: What the salt signified. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take it for a devoting of the site to perpetual barrenness; Clarke denies that sterility was in view at all, since no one cultivates a city, and makes it an emblem of perpetuity meant to fix the memorial of the deed.

Why the men of the tower went to the temple. Keil and Delitzsch insist it was for sanctuary rather than defence, since they too had dealt treacherously with Abimelech; Clarke reads the hold simply as the temple precincts, large enough to hold a thousand; Ellicott treats them as the garrison of Millo.

How the day's tactics differed from the previous engagement. Ellicott can only conjecture why three companies were used instead of four, and notes the successful interception at the gate; Keil and Delitzsch describe the division of labour between the gate party and the two in the field.
outliers: Clarke's and Ellicott's shared citation of Milan, sown with salt in the twelfth century, with Ellicott adding the salting of Coligny's house by royal command.
Gill's picture of the column climbing back with boughs on their shoulders, like men that were trees walking.
Ellicott's recollection of the bough-bearing soldiers in Macbeth.
themes: husbandmen caught in the field
a city sown with salt
sanctuary sought from a false god
a thousand under burning boughs

50.pericope_label: Thebez, the millstone, and the curse fulfilled

schools.summary: Gill gives Jerome's distance of thirteen miles for Thebez with a traveller's account of its ruins and marble, reports that the town had rebelled, notes that this tower stood within the city where the tower of Shechem had stood without, identifies the stone as a piece of the upper millstone, and observes at the close that the wickedness rendered was done against Gideon's own character and family, the evil of the Shechemites lying both in helping to kill the brethren and in crowning the murderer afterwards.

Henry takes Thebez for a small place dependent on Shechem and thinks Abimelech expected to repeat there what he had done at the temple stronghold, not considering that an idol-temple's tower lay more exposed to divine vengeance, since men who succeed in one desperate attempt think another not desperate; he notes that the peril of approaching a besieged wall became a standing warning but that God infatuates those he means to ruin. He finds a judgment in each circumstance of the death — a stone, as the brethren were killed upon one stone; the skull, vengeance aiming at the head that wore the usurped crown; and a woman's hand, which Abimelech saw and knew where Sisera died in ignorance — and draws from the smallness of the place that the mighty things of the world are often confounded by the weakest, concluding that a man who had some colour for chastising Shechem was destroyed when nothing would serve but that Thebez must be sacrificed to his rage.

Clarke notes that the phrase for the stone has been taken for a piece of a chariot wheel though the versions understand a millstone, complains that the old English rendering of the verb is nonsense for a plain statement that she fractured his skull, and recalls Plutarch on Pyrrhus killed by a tile thrown by a woman; he explains the dying order by the disgrace of being killed by a woman, quoting Seneca on the death of Hercules and suggesting that Abimelech also feared what his enemies might do to him alive; and he sums up the close by saying that both the fratricide and the unprincipled men who backed him had their iniquity visited on them, since man's judgment may be avoided but God's cannot, before returning to the fable and comparing it with the Sanskrit collection known in Europe as the fables of Pilpay.

Ellicott takes Thebez for one of the cities in the league of the covenant Baal, observes that the constant mention of towers through these chapters betrays a disturbed country not unlike England under King Stephen, concedes Abimelech physical courage and his father's impetuous energy, identifies the stone as the upper millstone or runner whirled over the fixed stone beneath, explains the old English crux as a printer's error for an intensive form, notes that the expedient did not save him from the taunt and that the ancients were sensitive about the manner of their death as Deborah's exultation over Sisera shows, and records that the army broke up at once as ancient armies did on a leader's death, quoting the judgment that with Abimelech expired this first abortive attempt at monarchy. Keil and Delitzsch place Thebez thirteen miles from Shechem on the road to Scythopolis, surviving in a village of similar name, and set the two verses of retribution side by side.

debates: What the stone was. Gill and Ellicott identify it as the upper millstone or runner; Clarke reports the alternative that the phrase means a piece of a chariot wheel, while noting that the versions support the millstone.

How the disputed English phrase about the skull should be read. Clarke calls the received rendering nonsense for a simple statement that she fractured his skull; Ellicott explains it as a printer's error for an intensive form familiar in older English.

Why Abimelech called for his armour-bearer. Clarke gives both the disgrace of dying by a woman's hand and the fear of what his enemies might do to him alive; Ellicott keeps to the point of honour and observes that the device failed, the taunt surviving him.
outliers: Clarke's parallel from Plutarch, of Pyrrhus killed at a siege by a tile thrown by a woman.
Henry's three circumstances of the death — a stone, a skull, and a woman's hand — each answering to something in the crime.
Stanley's judgment, quoted by Ellicott, that with Abimelech expired the first abortive attempt at monarchy, the true King of Israel being still far in the distance.
themes: a lesser town than the last
a millstone from the roof
not to be said a woman slew him
the curse of Jotham come home
